claim: Endothelial and skeletal muscle lineages arise from common embryonic progenitors.
source: Endothelial and skeletal muscle lineages arise from common embryonic progenitors.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Adult endothelial cells (ECs) and muscle stem cells (MuSCs; satellite cells) have been thought to possess distinct gene signatures and signaling pathways.
source: Despite their shared developmental origin, adult endothelial cells (ECs) and muscle stem cells (MuSCs; satellite cells) have been thought to possess distinct gene signatures and signaling pathways.
evidence: This represents the prevailing paradigm that the authors are challenging.

claim: MuSCs express low levels of canonical EC markers in mice.
source: We used several computational analyses including single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) to show that MuSCs express low levels of canonical EC markers in mice.
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq data and computational analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: MuSC survival is regulated by the VEGFA-FLT1 signaling pathway.
source: We demonstrate that MuSC survival is regulated by one such prototypic endothelial signaling pathway (VEGFA-FLT1).
evidence: Demonstrated through pharmacological and genetic experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: The FLT1-AKT1 axis is the key effector underlying VEGFA-mediated regulation of MuSC survival.
source: Using pharmacological and genetic gain- and loss-of-function studies, we identify the FLT1-AKT1 axis as the key effector underlying VEGFA-mediated regulation of MuSC survival.
evidence: Identified through gain- and loss-of-function studies presented in the results.

claim: The VEGFA-FLT1-AKT1 pathway promotes MuSC survival during muscle regeneration.
source: All together, our data support that the VEGFA-FLT1-AKT1 pathway promotes MuSC survival during muscle regeneration, and highlights how the minor expression of select transcripts is sufficient for affecting cell behavior.
evidence: Supported by multiple experimental approaches including in vitro and in vivo studies.

claim: Minor expression of select transcripts is sufficient for affecting cell behavior.
source: All together, our data support that the VEGFA-FLT1-AKT1 pathway promotes MuSC survival during muscle regeneration, and highlights how the minor expression of select transcripts is sufficient for affecting cell behavior.
evidence: This is a key conclusion drawn from the observation that low-level EC marker expression has functional consequences.

claim: Skeletal muscle and endothelial cells and their progenitors from the trunk and limbs are derived from the somites during early development.
source: Skeletal muscle and endothelial cells (ECs) and their progenitors from the trunk and limbs are derived from the somites during early developments.
evidence: This is established developmental biology knowledge.

claim: Bipotent progenitors exist which express both Pax3 and Flk1.
source: Previous works demonstrated the existence of bipotent progenitors which express both Pax3 and Flk1 (Eichmann et al., 1993; Kardon et al., 2002; Ema et al., 2006; Esner et al., 2006; Tozer et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Bipotent progenitors migrate into trunk and limb buds from ventrolateral region of the somites to generate MYOD(+) myogenic cells followed by skeletal muscle and PECAM1(+) ECs followed by vasculatures.
source: These bipotent progenitors migrate into trunk and limb buds from ventrolateral region of the somites to generate MYOD(+) myogenic cells followed by skeletal muscle and PECAM1(+) ECs followed by vasculatures (Hutcheson and Kardon, 2009; Kardon et al., 2002; Lagha et al., 2009; Mayeuf-Louchart et al., 2016; Mayeuf-Louchart et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations describing developmental processes.

claim: FLK1(+) cells give rise to myogenic cells during development and oncologic transformation.
source: In addition, FLK1(+) cells give rise to myogenic cells during development and oncologic transformation (Drummond and Hatley, 2018; Mayeuf-Louchart et al., 2014; Motoike et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Multipotent mesoangioblasts, vessel‐associated stem cells, have been identified in embryonic dorsal aorta.
source: Lastly, multipotent mesoangioblasts, vessel‐associated stem cells, have been identified in embryonic dorsal aorta (Minasi et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Minasi et al., 2002.

claim: Mesoangioblasts are able to differentiate into several types of mesodermal tissues including skeletal muscle and ECs.
source: These cells are able to differentiate into several types of mesodermal tissues including skeletal muscle and ECs (Roobrouck et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Roobrouck et al., 2011.

claim: Myogenic cells derived from mesoangioblasts show the same morphology as muscle satellite cells (MuSCs) and express myogenic and EC markers such as Myod, Cdh15, Kdr, and Cdh5.
source: Interestingly, these myogenic cells show the same morphology as muscle satellite cells (MuSCs), stem cell populations for skeletal muscle, and express a number of myogenic and EC markers such as Myod, Cdh15, Kdr, and Cdh5 (De Angelis et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to De Angelis et al., 1999.

claim: It is not clear whether adult MuSCs derived from bipotent progenitors still maintain canonical EC signals.
source: However, it is not clear whether adult MuSCs derived from these bipotent progenitors still maintain canonical EC signals.
evidence: This represents a knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: Blood vessel-associated myoendothelial cell progenitors that express both myogenic and EC markers have been identified in the interstitial spaces of both murine and human adult skeletal muscle.
source: Curiously, blood vessel-associated myoendothelial cell progenitors that express both myogenic and EC markers, and are able to differentiate into myogenic cells following transplantation have been identified in the interstitial spaces of both murine and human adult skeletal muscle (Tamaki et al., 2002; Zheng et al., 2007; Huang et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The relationship between myoendothelial cell progenitors and MuSCs remains unclear.
source: However, the relationship between these myoendothelial cell progenitors and MuSCs remains unclear.
evidence: This represents a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: VEGFA modulates many biological aspects including angiogenesis through its two receptors, FLT1 and FLK1.
source: Vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), specifically VEGFA modulates many biological aspects including angiogenesis through its two receptors, FLT1 and FLK1.
evidence: This is established knowledge about VEGFA signaling.

claim: FLK1 possesses stronger signaling capability and is the major signaling receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) for VEGFA.
source: Although FLK1 possesses stronger signaling capability and the major signaling receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) for VEGFA, FLT1 has considerably higher affinity for VEGF but weaker cytoplasmic signaling capability.
evidence: This is established knowledge about VEGF receptor properties.

claim: FLT1 has considerably higher affinity for VEGF but weaker cytoplasmic signaling capability.
source: Although FLK1 possesses stronger signaling capability and the major signaling receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) for VEGFA, FLT1 has considerably higher affinity for VEGF but weaker cytoplasmic signaling capability.
evidence: This is established knowledge about VEGF receptor properties.

claim: In normal tissue, FLT1 acts as a decoy receptor and a sink trap for VEGF thereby preventing excessive normal and pathological angiogenesis.
source: In normal tissue, FLT1 acts as a decoy receptor and a sink trap for VEGF thereby preventing excessive normal and pathological angiogenesis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about FLT1 function.

claim: There are two co-receptors for VEGFA (NRP1 and NRP2) that function with FLK1 to modulate VEGFA signaling.
source: In addition, there are two co-receptors for VEGFA (NRP1 and NRP2) that function with FLK1 to modulate VEGFA signaling.
evidence: This is established knowledge about VEGFA signaling components.

claim: VEGF signaling has been extensively studied for its role in development, proliferation, and survival of endothelial cells (ECs).
source: While VEGF signaling has been extensively studied for its role in development, proliferation, and survival of endothelial cells (ECs), its role in non-vascular systems such as neuron and bone has only recently been appreciated (Poesen et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2012; Okabe et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: The role of VEGF signaling in non-vascular systems such as neuron and bone has only recently been appreciated.
source: While VEGF signaling has been extensively studied for its role in development, proliferation, and survival of endothelial cells (ECs), its role in non-vascular systems such as neuron and bone has only recently been appreciated (Poesen et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2012; Okabe et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: Skeletal muscle tissue is the most abundant producer of VEGFA in the body.
source: Skeletal muscle tissue is the most abundant producer of VEGFA in the body.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact.

claim: VEGFA has been extensively studied in skeletal muscle fibers in models of Vegfa knockout mice.
source: It has already been extensively studied in the skeletal muscle fibers in models of Vegfa knockout mice (Tang et al., 2004; Wagner et al., 2006; Olfert et al., 2009) as well as Vegfa overexpression (Arsic et al., 2004; Yan et al., 2005; Messina et al., 2007; Bouchentouf et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: VEGFA has been extensively studied in skeletal muscle fibers in models of Vegfa overexpression.
source: It has already been extensively studied in the skeletal muscle fibers in models of Vegfa knockout mice (Tang et al., 2004; Wagner et al., 2006; Olfert et al., 2009) as well as Vegfa overexpression (Arsic et al., 2004; Yan et al., 2005; Messina et al., 2007; Bouchentouf et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: MuSCs mediate postnatal muscle growth and muscle regeneration.
source: Adult skeletal muscle also contains the tissue resident muscle stem cell population, termed MuSCs, which mediate postnatal muscle growth and muscle regeneration (Motohashi and Asakura, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about MuSC function with supporting citation.

claim: After muscle injury, quiescent MuSCs initiate proliferation to produce myogenic precursor cells, or myoblasts.
source: After muscle injury, quiescent MuSCs initiate proliferation to produce myogenic precursor cells, or myoblasts.
evidence: This describes the established process of muscle regeneration.

claim: Myoblasts undergo multiple rounds of cell division before terminal differentiation and formation of multinucleated myotubes by cell fusion.
source: The myoblasts undergo multiple rounds of cell division before terminal differentiation and formation of multinucleated myotubes by cell fusion.
evidence: This describes the established process of myogenic differentiation.

claim: MuSC-derived myoblasts express VEGFA, which has been shown to increase the proliferation of myoblasts.
source: Importantly, the MuSC-derived myoblasts also express VEGFA, which has been shown to increase the proliferation of myoblasts (Christov et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Christov et al., 2007.

claim: MuSCs express abundant VEGFA, which recruits ECs to establish vascular niche for MuSC self-renewal and maintenance.
source: Our data obtained from genetical model mice demonstrated that MuSCs express abundant VEGFA, which recruits ECs to establish vascular niche for MuSC self-renewal and maintenance (Verma et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: VEGFA and its receptors are expressed in the myoblast cell line, C2C12 cells.
source: In addition, VEGFA and its receptors are expressed in the myoblast cell line, C2C12 cells, and the signaling can induce cell migration and protect apoptotic cell during myogenic differentiation in vitro (Germani et al., 2003; Bryan et al., 2008; Mercatelli et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: VEGFA signaling can induce cell migration and protect apoptotic cell during myogenic differentiation in vitro.
source: In addition, VEGFA and its receptors are expressed in the myoblast cell line, C2C12 cells, and the signaling can induce cell migration and protect apoptotic cell during myogenic differentiation in vitro (Germani et al., 2003; Bryan et al., 2008; Mercatelli et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: It is not clear whether MuSCs also express VEGF receptors and if cell-autonomous VEGFA signaling plays an essential role in MuSC function during muscle regeneration in vivo.
source: However, it is not clear whether MuSCs also express VEGF receptors and if cell-autonomous VEGFA signaling plays an essential roles in MuSC function during muscle regeneration in vivo.
evidence: This represents a knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: Flt1 heterozygous gene knockout and conditional deletion of Flt1 in ECs display increased capillary density in skeletal muscle.
source: We have previously shown that Flt1 heterozygous gene knockout and conditional deletion of Flt1 in ECs display increased capillary density in skeletal muscle, indicating the essential roles for Flt1 in adult skeletal muscle.
evidence: This refers to the authors' previous work.

claim: When crossed with the Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) model mdx mice, Flt1 heterozygous and EC-specific conditional deletion mice show both histological and functional improvements of their dystrophic phenotypes.
source: More importantly, when crossed with the Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) model mdx mice, these mice show both histological and functional improvements of their dystrophic phenotypes.
evidence: This refers to the authors' previous work.

claim: The improvement in dystrophic phenotypes in mdx mice with Flt1 deletion was partly due to the effect of increased ECs leading to an increase in MuSCs.
source: This was partly due to the effect of increased ECs leading to an increase in MuSCs (Verma et al., 2010; Verma et al., 2019; Bosco et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to the authors' previous work.

claim: The effect of VEGFA on MuSC in vivo remained unknown prior to this study.
source: However, the effect of VEGFA on MuSC in vivo remained unknown.
evidence: This represents a knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: MuSCs express low levels of canonical EC markers including VEGF receptors using single cell transcriptomics.
source: We found that MuSCs express low levels of canonical EC markers including VEGF receptors using single cell transcriptomics.
evidence: This is a key finding from the scRNA-seq analysis.

claim: VEGFA has a drastic effect on MuSC survival via its receptor FLT1 by signaling through AKT1.
source: Therefore, we examined the effects of VEGFA on MuSCs and show that it has a drastic effect on cell survival in the via its receptor FLT1 by signaling through AKT1.
evidence: This is a key finding from the experimental studies.

claim: EC signatures in MuSCs have been seen in several gene expression data sets.
source: EC signatures in MuSCs has been seen in several gene expression data sets (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–1D, Supplementary file 1; Fukada et al., 2007; Charville et al., 2015; Ryall et al., 2015; van Velthoven et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by references to figures and citations to previous studies.

claim: Single muscle fibers routinely have EC fragments attached to the fiber.
source: We found that single muscle fibers routinely have ECs fragments attached to the fiber (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G) and so we removed such fibers based on Flk1GFP expression from the samples collected for sequencing.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental procedures with supporting figure.

claim: MuSCs express minimal but reliable levels of canonical EC genes such as Pecam1, Cdh5, Kdr, and Flt1.
source: We surveyed for canonical genes for each cell type (Figure 1B) and found minimal but reliable expression of canonical ECs genes such as Pecam1, Cdh5, Kdr, and Flt1 in MuSCs.
evidence: Supported by bulk RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Quiescent and activated MuSCs can be reliably delineated via side and forward scatter in FACS.
source: We could reliably delineate injured and activated MuSCs via side and forward scatter (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H and I).
evidence: Supported by FACS data shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: MuSCs showed low overlap between D0 and D3 owing to the different stages of the myogenic differentiation cycle in scRNA-seq analysis.
source: In the aggregated dataset, the MuSCs showed low overlap between D0 and D3 owing to the different stages of the myogenic differentiation cycle, while the ECs clusters showed near perfect overlap (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: Supported by UMAP visualization in Figure 1C and D.

claim: EC clusters showed near perfect overlap between D0 and D3 in scRNA-seq analysis.
source: In the aggregated dataset, the MuSCs showed low overlap between D0 and D3 owing to the different stages of the myogenic differentiation cycle, while the ECs clusters showed near perfect overlap (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: Supported by UMAP visualization in Figure 1C and D.

claim: Drastic morphological changes in ECs have been shown during muscle regeneration.
source: While drastic morphological changes in ECs have been shown during muscle regeneration (Hardy et al., 2016), transcriptomic changes are much more tapered, especially compared with MuSCs (Latroche et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Transcriptomic changes in ECs during muscle regeneration are much more tapered compared with MuSCs.
source: While drastic morphological changes in ECs have been shown during muscle regeneration (Hardy et al., 2016), transcriptomic changes are much more tapered, especially compared with MuSCs (Latroche et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Latroche et al., 2017.

claim: scRNA-seq data were able to recapitulate the minimal expression of canonical EC genes in the MuSC clusters such as Cdh5.
source: Importantly, data from scRNA-seq were able to recapitulate the minimal expression of canonical EC genes in the MuSC clusters such as Cdh5 (Figure 1E) as seen in our Bulk RNA-seq results (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by comparison of scRNA-seq and bulk RNA-seq data.

claim: Vegf receptors Flk1 (Kdr) and Flt1 are expressed in MuSC clusters in scRNA-seq data.
source: These included the Vegf receptors Flk1 (Kdr) and Flt1 (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The presence of eGFP in MuSCs and tdTomato in ECs in scRNA-seq data is due to ambient-free mRNA from digested cells intrinsic to droplet-based single-cell sequencing platforms.
source: Therefore, we hypothesized that this was due to the ambient-free mRNA from the digested cells that is intrinsic to any droplet based single-cell sequencing platform.
evidence: This is a hypothesis to explain the unexpected finding, later tested with SoupX.

claim: After SoupX background subtraction, eGFP expression in the MuSC fraction and tdTomato expression in the EC fraction was decreased but sustained.
source: We observed decreased but sustained eGFP expression in the MuSC fraction and tdTomato expression in the EC fraction after SoupX subtraction (Figure 1—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: Supported by SoupX analysis results shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: EC signatures such as Cdh5 expression in the MuSC fraction was sustained after SoupX subtraction.
source: In addition, the EC signatures such as Cdh5 expression in the MuSC fraction was also sustained.
evidence: Supported by SoupX analysis results.

claim: MuSCs contain mRNAs from canonical EC genes.
source: These results conclude that MuSCs contain mRNAs from canonical ECs genes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the scRNA-seq and background subtraction analysis.

claim: Canonical EC genes such as Cdh5, Flt1 and Flk1 are broadly expressed in myogenic cells.
source: We showed that the canonical EC genes, such as Cdh5, Flt1 and Flk1 were broadly expressed in the myogenic cells in our dataset (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: EC prototypic markers such as Flt1 are broadly expressed with small amounts in MuSCs in a previously published dataset with 2,232 myogenic cells.
source: We noticed that EC prototypic markers such as Flt1 are broadly expressed with small amounts in MuSCs.
evidence: Supported by re-analysis of published dataset (Torre et al., 2018; De Micheli et al., 2020).

claim: EC prototypic markers such as Cdh5, Flt1, and Kdr are clearly expressed in MuSCs using microarrays and Bulk-RNA-seq from different laboratories.
source: Complementary data from different laboratories showed the clear expression of EC prototypic markers such as Cdh5, Flt1, and Kdr, using microarrays and Bulk-RNA-seq (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B; Fukada et al., 2007; Ryall et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by analysis of published datasets with citations.

claim: Flt1 may be transiently upregulated during the early activation process in MuSCs.
source: RNA-seq data from fixed quiescent, early activated and late activated MuSCs show that Flt1 may be transiently upregulated during the early activation process (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C; Yue et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by analysis of published RNA-seq data with citation.

claim: EC genes such as Kdr and Pecam1 are actively transcribed by MuSCs as detected in TU-tagged MuSC nascent RNA samples.
source: Interestingly, we were able to detect EC genes such as Kdr and Pecam1 in the TU-tagged MuSC samples indicating that they were actively transcribed by MuSCs (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by analysis of TU-tagged nascent RNA data.

claim: Vegfr genes (Kdr, Flt1, Nrp1, and Nrp2) are expressed in MuSCs as verified by RT-qPCR.
source: We also verified the expression of Vegfr genes (Kdr, Flt1, Nrp1, and Nrp2) in MuSCs using RT-qPCR (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Flt1 expression in MuSCs was verified by in situ hybridization using RNAScope on whole muscle fiber.
source: In addition, we verified the expression of Flt1 by performing in situ hybridization using RNAScope on MuSC on whole muscle fiber, which we currently believe to be the gold standard for expression studies (Figure 1H).
evidence: Supported by RNAScope data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: In MuSC-derived myoblasts, NRP1 and NRP2 expression was detectable with comparable intensity compared with EC cell line.
source: Finally, in MuSC-derived myoblasts, NRP1and NRP2 expression was detectable with comparable intensity compared with EC cell line, while FLT1 expression was detectable with lower intensity compared with EC cell line (Figure 1I).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: FLT1 expression was detectable with lower intensity in MuSC-derived myoblasts compared with EC cell line.
source: Finally, in MuSC-derived myoblasts, NRP1and NRP2 expression was detectable with comparable intensity compared with EC cell line, while FLT1 expression was detectable with lower intensity compared with EC cell line (Figure 1I).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: PECAM1, VE-Cadherin and FLK1 expression, which was clearly detected in EC cell line, was undetectable in myoblasts.
source: By contrast, PECAM1, VE-Cadherin and FLK1 expression, which was clearly detected in EC cell line, was undetectable level in myoblasts.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: There are both transcripts of EC canonical genes and EC canonical proteins in MuSCs.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that there are both transcripts of these EC canonical genes and EC canonical proteins in MuSCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence including RNA-seq, qPCR, RNAScope, and immunostaining.

claim: Treatment with VEGFA could increase proliferation of MuSC-derived myoblasts at low dose but inhibit proliferation at high dose of VEGFA.
source: We found that treatment with VEGFA could increase proliferation of MuSC-derived myoblasts at low dose but inhibit proliferation at high dose of VEGFA, a phenomenon that has been previously described in ECs (Noren et al., 2016; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by proliferation assay data with citation to similar phenomenon in ECs.

claim: VEGFA had no effect on differentiation of MuSC-derived myoblasts as evaluated by myosin heavy chain (MyHC) staining, fusion index and RT-qPCR.
source: We saw no effect on differentiation by VEGFA as evaluated by myosin heavy chain (MyHC) staining, fusion index and RT-qPCR (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: Supported by multiple differentiation assays shown in supplementary figures.

claim: VEGFA could significantly increase survival of myoblasts following UV-mediated apoptotic cell death induction as judged by crystal violet staining.
source: By contrast, crystal violet staining showed that VEGFA could significantly increase survival as judged by number of myoblasts following UV-mediated apoptotic cell death induction (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: Supported by crystal violet staining data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: MuSCs are the predominant cells that secrete VEGFA in skeletal muscle.
source: We had previously shown that MuSCs are the predominant cells that secrete VEGFA in skeletal muscle (Verma et al., 2018) and while adding exogenous VEGFA did not improve cell survival, blocking VEGFA via a soluble form of FLT1-FC increased the number of apoptotic and necrotic myoblasts in vitro (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work and new data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Blocking VEGFA via a soluble form of FLT1-FC increased the number of apoptotic and necrotic myoblasts in vitro.
source: We had previously shown that MuSCs are the predominant cells that secrete VEGFA in skeletal muscle (Verma et al., 2018) and while adding exogenous VEGFA did not improve cell survival, blocking VEGFA via a soluble form of FLT1-FC increased the number of apoptotic and necrotic myoblasts in vitro (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: Supported by Annexin V assay data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Inhibiting FLT1 via blocking antibody greatly decreased the survival of myoblasts following thapsigargin induction.
source: By contrast, blocking FLT1 via blocking antibody greatly decreased the survival of myoblasts following thapsigargin induction (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by apoptosis assay data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Inhibiting FLK1 had no effect on myoblast survival following thapsigargin induction.
source: Surprisingly, inhibiting FLK1, the major signaling RTK for VEGFA, had no effect on myoblasts survival following thapsigargin induction (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by apoptosis assay data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: In vitro 4-OHT-mediated genetic deletion of Flt1 (MuSC-Flt1Δ/Δ) resulted in down-regulation of Flt1 RNA and FLT1 protein expression.
source: In vitro 4-OHT-mediated genetic deletion of Flt1 (MuSC-Flt1Δ/Δ) resulted in down-regulation of Flt1 RNA and FLT1 protein expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 1I and J), and increased spontaneous apoptotic cell death even without induction of apoptosis (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR and immunostaining data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Genetic deletion of Flt1 in myoblasts increased spontaneous apoptotic cell death even without induction of apoptosis.
source: In vitro 4-OHT-mediated genetic deletion of Flt1 (MuSC-Flt1Δ/Δ) resulted in down-regulation of Flt1 RNA and FLT1 protein expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 1I and J), and increased spontaneous apoptotic cell death even without induction of apoptosis (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by Annexin V assay data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Flt1 deletion did not affect cell proliferation assessed by EdU staining or myogenic differentiation assessed by MyHC staining.
source: By contrast, Flt1 deletion did not affect cell proliferation assessed by EdU staining or myogenic differentiation assessed by MyHC staining (Figure 2—figure supplement 1K–M).
evidence: Supported by EdU and MyHC staining data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: MuSC-Flt1Δ/Δ myoblasts had increased apoptosis following thapsigargin induction that was not responsive to exogenous VEGFA.
source: When thapsigargin-induced apoptosis was induced, the MuSC-Flt1Δ/Δ myoblasts had increased apoptosis that was not responsive to exogenous VEGFA (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by Annexin V assay data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: In ECs, VEGFA is known to protect cells from apoptosis via AKT1.
source: In ECs, VEGFA is known to protect cells from apoptosis via AKT1 (Domigan et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies in ECs.

claim: It is not known whether VEGFA can activate AKT1 in MuSC-derived myoblasts.
source: However, it is not known whether VEGFA can similarly activate AKT1 in MuSC-derived myoblasts.
evidence: This represents a knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: The role of AKT1 in apoptosis in myoblasts has not been well characterized.
source: While the role of AKT1 has been explored in proliferation and differentiation in myoblasts, its role in apoptosis has not been well characterized (Loiben et al., 2017).
evidence: This represents a knowledge gap with supporting citation.

claim: Exogenous VEGFA could induce AKT1 phosphorylation (pAKT1) in MuSC-derived myoblasts.
source: We found that exogenous VEGFA could induce AKT1 phosphorylation (pAKT1) (Figure 2G and H, Figure 2—figure supplement 1N and O).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and Western blot data shown in figures.

claim: VEGFA-induced AKT1 phosphorylation was blunted in MuSC-Flt1Δ/Δ myoblasts and was no longer responsive to VEGFA.
source: This response was blunted in MuSC-Flt1Δ/Δ myoblasts and was no longer responsive to VEGFA (Figure 2G and H, Figure 2—figure supplement 1N and O).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and Western blot data shown in figures.

claim: Overexpression of E4ORF1 or MyrAKT1 improved myoblast survival compared with the control in vitro following induction of apoptosis via thapsigargin.
source: We found that overexpression of either of these genes improved cell survival compared with the control in vitro following induction of apoptosis via thapsigargin (Figure 2I).
evidence: Supported by Annexin V assay data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: FLT1-AKT1 is the cascade linking VEGFA to apoptosis in MuSC-derived myoblasts during muscle regeneration.
source: These data establish FLT1-AKT1 as the cascade linking VEGFA to apoptosis in MuSC-derived myoblasts during muscle regeneration (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: Endogenous and exogenous VEGFA have been shown to regulate cell survival and protect ECs from apoptosis.
source: Endogenous and exogenous VEGFA have been shown to regulate cell survival and protect ECs from apoptosis (Gerber et al., 1998; Lee et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: MuSC-derived myoblasts from Pax7+/tdT:Vegfa+/Hyper mice showed around 2.8-fold increased expression of Vegfa but not the Vegfr genes compared with myoblasts from wild-type mice.
source: MuSC-derived myoblasts from Pax7+/tdT:Vegfa+/Hyper mice showed around 2.8-fold increased expression of Vegfa but not the Vegfr genes compared with myoblasts from wild-type mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in supplementary figure.

claim: MuSCs from Pax7+/tdT:Vegfa+/Hyper mice showed decreased cell death in regenerating muscle by 1 day following BaCl2 injection.
source: Interestingly, while treatment with VEGFA alone had no effect on apoptosis in vitro, the MuSCs from Pax7+/tdT:Vegfa+/Hyper mice showed decreased cell death in regenerating muscle by 1 day following BaCl2 injection (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by Annexin V staining data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Single muscle fibers from Pax7+/tdT:Vegfa+/Hyper mice showed increased number of MuSCs compared with those from Pax7+/tdT:Vegfa+/+ mice by 28 days following BaCl2 injection.
source: Consequently, single muscle fibers from Pax7+/tdT:Vegfa+/Hyper mice showed increased number of MuSCs, compared with those from Pax7+/tdT:Vegfa+/+ mice by 28 days following BaCl2 injection (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by MuSC quantification data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Muscle regeneration was promoted in Vegfa+/Hyper mice in the early (14 days) and late (28 days) muscle repair processes as judged by fiber diameter and increase in eMHC(+) regenerating muscle fibers.
source: In addition, muscle regeneration was promoted in Vegfa+/Hyper mice in the early (14 days) and late (28 days) muscle repair processes as judged by fiber diameter and increase in eMHC(+) regenerating muscle fibers (Figure 3E and F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–F).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis data shown in figures.

claim: Deletion of Vegfa in MuSCs in the MuSC-VegfaΔ/Δ mouse muscle led to an increase in the proportion of dead MuSCs following BaCl2 injection.
source: We noticed that deletion of Vegfa in MuSCs in the MuSC-VegfaΔ/Δ mouse muscle led to an increase in the proportion of dead MuSCs following BaCl2 injection (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by Annexin V staining data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The number of MuSCs in the MuSC-VegfaΔ/Δ muscle were significantly reduced following recovery after injury without difference in the MuSC numbers in MuSC-VegfaΔ/Δ muscle at homeostasis.
source: Consequently, the number of MuSCs in the MuSC-VegfaΔ/Δ muscle were significantly reduced following recovery after injury without difference in the MuSC numbers in MuSC-VegfaΔ/Δ muscle at homeostasis (Figure 3H).
evidence: Supported by MuSC quantification data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: MuSC-VegfaΔ/Δ muscle had a regenerative defect as indicated by the shift in fiber size distribution, decrease in the size of regenerating eMHC(+) fiber and increased adipose following muscle injury.
source: In addition, the muscle had a regenerative defect as indicated by the shift in fiber size distribution, decrease in the size of regenerating eMHC(+) fiber and increased adipose following muscle injury (Figure 3B, I and J, Figure 3—figure supplement 2B–E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis data shown in multiple figures.

claim: Cell intrinsic VEGFA improves cell survival of MuSCs.
source: These data indicate that cell intrinsic VEGFA improves cell survival of MuSCs and that loss of MuSC-derived VEGFA results in reduced muscle regeneration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the MuSC-VegfaΔ/Δ experiments.

claim: Loss of MuSC-derived VEGFA results in reduced muscle regeneration.
source: These data indicate that cell intrinsic VEGFA improves cell survival of MuSCs and that loss of MuSC-derived VEGFA results in reduced muscle regeneration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the MuSC-VegfaΔ/Δ experiments.

claim: Loss of Flt1 in MuSCs resulted in increased cell death during early regeneration.
source: As seen in vitro, we found that loss of Flt1 in MuSCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1I and J) resulted in increased cell death during early regeneration (Figure 3K).
evidence: Supported by Annexin V staining data shown in Figure 3K.

claim: Single muscle fibers from MuSC-Flt1Δ/Δ mice showed a decreased number of MuSCs compared with those from MuSC-Flt1+/+ mice by 28 days following BaCl2 injection.
source: Consequently, single muscle fibers from MuSC-Flt1Δ/Δ mice showed a decreased number of MuSCs, compared with those from MuSC-Flt1+/+ mice by 28 days following BaCl2 injection (Figure 3L).
evidence: Supported by MuSC quantification data shown in Figure 3L.

claim: There was no significant muscle phenotype in MuSC-Flt1Δ/Δ muscle at homeostasis.
source: There was no significant muscle phenotype in MuSC-Flt1Δ/Δ muscle at homeostasis (Figure 3B, M and N).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis data shown in figures.

claim: Following injury, the MuSC-Flt1Δ/Δ muscle had a modest regenerative defect as indicated by the shift in fiber size distribution following muscle injury and decrease in size of eMHC(+) regenerating fibers.
source: However, following injury, the MuSC-Flt1Δ/Δ muscle had a modest regenerative defect as indicated by the shift in fiber size distribution following muscle injury and decrease in size of eMHC(+) regenerating fibers (Figure 3B, M and N, Figure 3—figure supplement 2F–J, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis data shown in multiple figures.

claim: Angiogenic defects have been reported in the mdx mice as well as in golden retrieval muscular dystrophy (GRMD; canine model of DMD).
source: While angiogenic defects have been reported in the mdx mice as well as in golden retrieval muscular dystrophy (GRMD; canine model of DMD) (Verma et al., 2010; Latroche et al., 2015; Verma et al., 2019; Kodippili et al., 2021; Podkalicka et al., 2021), it is not clear whether VEGF family and its receptors are implicated in human dystrophinopathies.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: It is not clear whether VEGF family and its receptors are implicated in human dystrophinopathies.
source: While angiogenic defects have been reported in the mdx mice as well as in golden retrieval muscular dystrophy (GRMD; canine model of DMD) (Verma et al., 2010; Latroche et al., 2015; Verma et al., 2019; Kodippili et al., 2021; Podkalicka et al., 2021), it is not clear whether VEGF family and its receptors are implicated in human dystrophinopathies.
evidence: This represents a knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: Vegfa was downregulated in both mdx and GRMD models.
source: Vegfa was downregulated in both models (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by microarray analysis data shown in supplementary figure.

claim: Flt1 was downregulated in GRMD but not mdx muscles.
source: Flt1 was also downregulated in GRMD but not mdx muscles.
evidence: Supported by microarray analysis data.

claim: Vegfa expression was increased after an acute bout of exercise in microarray data from muscle biopsies.
source: In the microarray data, Vegfa expression was increased after an acute bout of exercise, and Vegfa expression was reduced in ALS muscle, BMD muscle, as well as both early and late phases of DMD muscle (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by microarray analysis data shown in supplementary figure.

claim: Vegfa expression was reduced in ALS muscle, BMD muscle, as well as both early and late phases of DMD muscle.
source: In the microarray data, Vegfa expression was increased after an acute bout of exercise, and Vegfa expression was reduced in ALS muscle, BMD muscle, as well as both early and late phases of DMD muscle (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by microarray analysis data shown in supplementary figure.

claim: Vegfa expression is decreased in dystrophinopathy.
source: These data indicate that Vegfa expression is decreased in dystrophinopathy, and thus increasing VEGFA may be a therapeutic target for DMD.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the microarray analysis.

claim: Increasing VEGFA may be a therapeutic target for DMD.
source: These data indicate that Vegfa expression is decreased in dystrophinopathy, and thus increasing VEGFA may be a therapeutic target for DMD.
evidence: This is a therapeutic implication drawn from the data.

claim: mdx:MuSC-Flt1Δ/Δ mice showed a significant decrease in fiber diameter at 3 months of age.
source: Importantly, we found a significant decrease in fiber diameter, increased fibrosis and CD31(+) capillary density (Figure 4B–D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D) in TA muscle.
evidence: Supported by histological analysis data shown in figures.

claim: mdx:MuSC-Flt1Δ/Δ mice showed increased fibrosis at 3 months of age.
source: Importantly, we found a significant decrease in fiber diameter, increased fibrosis and CD31(+) capillary density (Figure 4B–D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D) in TA muscle.
evidence: Supported by histological analysis data shown in figures.

claim: mdx:MuSC-Flt1Δ/Δ mice showed decreased CD31(+) capillary density at 3 months of age.
source: Importantly, we found a significant decrease in fiber diameter, increased fibrosis and CD31(+) capillary density (Figure 4B–D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D) in TA muscle.
evidence: Supported by histological analysis data shown in figures.

claim: mdx:MuSC-Flt1Δ/Δ mice showed a physiological decrease in muscle perfusion as shown by laser Doppler flow at 12 months.
source: This was accompanied by a physiological decrease in muscle perfusion as shown by laser Doppler flow at 12 months (Figure 4E) as well as a functional decline in muscle strength as judged by grip strength both acutely and chronically (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by laser Doppler flow data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: mdx:MuSC-Flt1Δ/Δ mice showed a functional decline in muscle strength as judged by grip strength both acutely and chronically.
source: This was accompanied by a physiological decrease in muscle perfusion as shown by laser Doppler flow at 12 months (Figure 4E) as well as a functional decline in muscle strength as judged by grip strength both acutely and chronically (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by grip strength data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: mdx:Vegfa+/Hyper mice showed a significant increase in fiber diameter at 3 months of age.
source: By contrast, when we crossed the Vegfa+/Hyper mice with mdx mice (Figure 4A), we noticed a significant increase in fiber diameter, increase in capillary density and decreased fibrosis (Figure 4G–I, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–F) in both TA and diaphragm muscle of mdx:Vegfa+/Hyper mice.
evidence: Supported by histological analysis data shown in figures.

claim: mdx:Vegfa+/Hyper mice showed an increase in capillary density at 3 months of age.
source: By contrast, when we crossed the Vegfa+/Hyper mice with mdx mice (Figure 4A), we noticed a significant increase in fiber diameter, increase in capillary density and decreased fibrosis (Figure 4G–I, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–F) in both TA and diaphragm muscle of mdx:Vegfa+/Hyper mice.
evidence: Supported by histological analysis data shown in figures.

claim: mdx:Vegfa+/Hyper mice showed decreased fibrosis at 3 months of age.
source: By contrast, when we crossed the Vegfa+/Hyper mice with mdx mice (Figure 4A), we noticed a significant increase in fiber diameter, increase in capillary density and decreased fibrosis (Figure 4G–I, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–F) in both TA and diaphragm muscle of mdx:Vegfa+/Hyper mice.
evidence: Supported by histological analysis data shown in figures.

claim: mdx:Vegfa+/Hyper mice showed a physiological increase in muscle perfusion as shown by laser Doppler flow at 12 months age.
source: This was accompanied by a physiological increase in muscle perfusion as shown by laser Doppler flow at 12 months age (Figure 4J) as well as a functional increase in muscle strength as judged by grip strength (Figure 4K) without a change in body mass (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by laser Doppler flow data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: mdx:Vegfa+/Hyper mice showed a functional increase in muscle strength as judged by grip strength.
source: This was accompanied by a physiological increase in muscle perfusion as shown by laser Doppler flow at 12 months age (Figure 4J) as well as a functional increase in muscle strength as judged by grip strength (Figure 4K) without a change in body mass (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by grip strength data shown in Figure 4K.

claim: The Vegfa+/Hyper mouse had lower number of apoptotic MuSC when the muscle was injured acutely with BaCl2.
source: Lastly, when the muscle was injured acutely, with BaCl2, the Vegfa+/Hyper mouse had lower number of apoptotic MuSC (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: Supported by Caspase-3 staining data shown in supplementary figure.

claim: VEGFA-FLT1 axis is a therapeutic target for the pathology seen in the DMD model mdx mice.
source: These data indicate that VEGFA-FLT1 axis is a therapeutic target for the pathology seen in the DMD model mdx mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mdx experiments.

claim: Deep reads can significantly reduce the effect of technical noise in scRNA-seq and improve estimation of minor transcriptional state of a given cell.
source: Since deep reads can significantly reduce the effect of the technical noise in scRNA-seq, it can improve estimation of minor transcriptional state of a given cell (Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2020.

claim: Similar phenomenon of EC marker expression in myogenic cells during development and existence of blood-vessel-associated myoendothelial cells in the adult skeletal muscle have been previously described.
source: While similar phenomenon in myogenic cells during development and existence of blood-vessel-associated myoendothelial cells in the adult skeletal muscle have been previously described, no functional follow up as been performed leading to the questions whether these minor expression profiles were artifacts or functional (De Angelis et al., 1999; Minasi et al., 2002; Tamaki et al., 2002; Zheng et al., 2007; Roobrouck et al., 2011; Huang et al., 2014; Charville et al., 2015; Goel et al., 2017; Giordani et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: No functional follow up has been performed on EC marker expression in myogenic cells, leading to questions whether these minor expression profiles were artifacts or functional.
source: While similar phenomenon in myogenic cells during development and existence of blood-vessel-associated myoendothelial cells in the adult skeletal muscle have been previously described, no functional follow up as been performed leading to the questions whether these minor expression profiles were artifacts or functional (De Angelis et al., 1999; Minasi et al., 2002; Tamaki et al., 2002; Zheng et al., 2007; Roobrouck et al., 2011; Huang et al., 2014; Charville et al., 2015; Goel et al., 2017; Giordani et al., 2019).
evidence: This represents a knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: Flt1 exerts a biological function even at a low expression level.
source: We found that Flt1 indeed exerts a biological function even at a low expression.
evidence: This is a key conclusion from the functional studies.

claim: Signaling through VEGFA-FLT1-AKT1 can improve cell survival in MuSCs both in vivo and in vitro.
source: Signaling through VEGFA-FLT1-AKT1 can improve cell survival in MuSCs both in vivo and in vitro.
evidence: This is a key conclusion from the study.

claim: The finding of EC prototype markers expressed in MuSC calls into question the genes that we use to specify cellular identities.
source: On a grander scale, our finding of EC prototype markers expressed in MuSC calls into two questions (1) the genes that we used to specify cellular identities and (2) the cellular identity of MuSCs and ECs.
evidence: This is a broader implication of the findings.

claim: The finding of EC prototype markers expressed in MuSC calls into question the cellular identity of MuSCs and ECs.
source: On a grander scale, our finding of EC prototype markers expressed in MuSC calls into two questions (1) the genes that we used to specify cellular identities and (2) the cellular identity of MuSCs and ECs.
evidence: This is a broader implication of the findings.

claim: It is possible that EC mRNAs are results of transcription from the cell or a result of mRNA transfer from neighboring cells.
source: It is also possible that EC mRNAs are results of transcription from the cell or a result of mRNA transfer from neighboring cells (Desrochers et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism with supporting citation.

claim: The transmission of tdTomato mRNA and protein from Pax7+/CreERT2:R26R+/tdT mice has been recently shown via exosome.
source: Of note, the transmission of tdTomato mRNA and protein from Pax7+/CreERT2:R26R+/tdTmice used in this study has been recently shown via exosome, opening up the possibility of transmission of other mRNA from MuSC to ECs (Murach et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Murach et al., 2020.

claim: There is a possibility of transmission of mRNA from MuSC to ECs via exosomes.
source: Of note, the transmission of tdTomato mRNA and protein from Pax7+/CreERT2:R26R+/tdTmice used in this study has been recently shown via exosome, opening up the possibility of transmission of other mRNA from MuSC to ECs (Murach et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculation based on recent findings.

claim: It is possible that there is a permissive chromatin state that allows for expression of reciprocal genes in MuSCs and ECs.
source: Therefore, it is possible that there is a permissive chromatin state that allows for expression of reciprocal genes in the two populations.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism based on developmental origins.

claim: FLK1(+) or VE-cadherin(+) cells can contribute to myogenic cells in vitro and after cell transplantation.
source: Along the lines of these observations, FLK1(+) or VE-cadherin(+) cells can contribute to myogenic cells in vitro and after cell transplantation (Tamaki et al., 2002; Le Grand et al., 2004; Zheng et al., 2007; Huang et al., 2014), and during development (Motoike et al., 2003; Mayeuf-Louchart et al., 2014; Drummond and Hatley, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: FLK1(+) or VE-cadherin(+) cells can contribute to myogenic cells during development.
source: Along the lines of these observations, FLK1(+) or VE-cadherin(+) cells can contribute to myogenic cells in vitro and after cell transplantation (Tamaki et al., 2002; Le Grand et al., 2004; Zheng et al., 2007; Huang et al., 2014), and during development (Motoike et al., 2003; Mayeuf-Louchart et al., 2014; Drummond and Hatley, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The PDGFRα(-)FLK1(+) population exhibited restricted potential to differentiate into the MuSCs in injured muscle.
source: Important notion is that the PDGFRα(-)FLK1(+) population exhibited restricted potential to differentiate into the MuSCs in injured muscle (Sakurai et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sakurai et al., 2008.

claim: In zebrafish, exogenous expression of Etv2 in the fast muscle can lead to transdifferentiation of muscle fibers into functional vessels.
source: Interestingly, in the zebrafish, exogenous expression of Etv2 in the fast muscle can lead to transdifferentiation of muscle fibers into functional vessels so there is evidence of cell fate flexibility (Veldman et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Veldman et al., 2013.

claim: Human skeletal muscle cells showed the highest amenability for EC induction following infection with ETV2 lentivirus vector among five human cell types tested.
source: Among them, human skeletal muscle cells showed the highest amenability for this EC induction following infection with ETV2 lentivirus vector (Yan et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yan et al., 2019.

claim: Etv2-deficient vascular progenitors can differentiate into skeletal muscle cells.
source: Conversely, Etv2-deficient vascular progenitors can differentiate into skeletal muscle cells (Chestnut et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chestnut et al., 2020.

claim: VEGFB is expressed in the MuSCs and muscle fiber.
source: While PGF is not normally expressed in adult tissues, VEGFB is expressed in the MuSCs and muscle fiber (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from unpublished data.

claim: The VEGFB-FLT1 axis has been shown to inhibit apoptosis in retina and brain cells in mouse models of ocular neurodegeneration and stroke.
source: Importantly, the VEGFB-FLT1 axis has also been shown to inhibit apoptosis in retina and brain cells in mouse models of ocular neurodegeneration and stroke (Li et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al., 2008.

claim: The long-term consequences of in vivo deletion of Flt1 in the MuSC compartment were modest compared with deletion of Vegfa in the MuSCs unless crossing with mdx mice.
source: Despite drastic effect of VEGFA-FLT1 on apoptosis in vitro, the long-term consequences of in vivo deletion of Flt1 in the MuSC compartment were modest compared with deletion of Vegfa in the MuSCs unless crossing with mdx mice.
evidence: This is an observation from the in vivo experiments.

claim: In the steady state, the MuSC turnover may be low enough that the apoptotic stress burden is low.
source: Although Vegfa is required for both MuSC survival and recruitment of vascular niche (Verma et al., 2018), in the steady state, the MuSC turnover may be low enough that the apoptotic stress burden is low.
evidence: This is a speculation to explain the modest phenotype at homeostasis.

claim: VEGFA improves cell survival during the proliferative stage following injury in mdx:Vegfa+/Hyper mice.
source: We demonstrated that VEGFA improves cell survival during the proliferative stage following injury in mdx:Vegfa+/Hyper mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the mdx experiments.

claim: MuSCs obtained from mdx mice engraft to a much lesser degree than those from WT mice in transplantation experiments.
source: The evidence that MuSC survival is impaired comes indirectly from transplantation experiments where MuSCs obtained from mdx mice engraft to a much lesser degree than those from WT mice (Boldrin et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Boldrin et al., 2015.

claim: VEGFA is expressed in MuSC and inflammatory cells.
source: They showed that VEGFA is expressed in expression in MuSC and inflammatory cells.
evidence: This refers to findings from Groppa et al., 2023.

claim: VEGFA increased MuSC proliferation through KDR (FLK1) according to Groppa et al.
source: In addition, VEGFA increased MuSC proliferation through KDR (FLK1).
evidence: This refers to findings from Groppa et al., 2023.

claim: Deletion of MuSC derived VEGFA lead to an increase in TUNEL(+) apoptotic MuSC according to Groppa et al.
source: They also found that deletion of MuSC derived VEGFA lead to an increase in TUNEL(+) apoptotic MuSC.
evidence: This refers to findings from Groppa et al., 2023.

claim: MuSC lacking KDR showed asymmetrical division deficits and limit MuSC proliferation resulting in impaired tissue regeneration according to Chen et al.
source: The role of KDR in MuSC was also corroborated by Chen et.al who showed that MuSC lacking KDR showed asymmetrical division deficits and limit MuSC proliferation resulting in impaired tissue regeneration.
evidence: This refers to findings from Chen et al., 2022.

claim: VEGFA and FLT1 targeted therapies are being explored as both pro- and anti-angiogenic therapies for several indications including retinal degeneration, cancer, pre-eclampsia, and neuromuscular diseases.
source: VEGFA and FLT1 targeted therapies are being explored as both pro- and anti-angiogenic therapies for several indications including retinal degeneration, cancer, pre-eclampsia, and neuromuscular diseases (Bae et al., 2005; Verma et al., 2010; Mac Gabhann et al., 2010; Keifer et al., 2014; Verma et al., 2019; Bosco et al., 2021; Xin et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: It will be important to ascertain the MuSC-specific effects of VEGFA and FLT1 as these therapies mature.
source: As these therapies mature, it will be important to ascertain the MuSC-specific effects of VEGFA and FLT1.
evidence: This is a forward-looking statement about the implications of the findings.
